paras: The killing of Tom Johnson was the shooting of a young Black man by four masked men at a home near Joiner's store in Clay County in February 1881. Black residents charged two sons of a local man, Joe Joiner, and two other young men with the crime, but a coroner's jury found that Johnson died at the hands of unknown parties.

On the night of the killing the Black residents of the neighborhood had held a gathering and then dispersed to their homes. Johnson went to the home of Jere Johnson, described as "an old acquaintance and friend."
While he was there, "a body consisting of four masked men" came on him and shot him, and he appears to have died of his wounds. A woman in the house was also "slightly shot."

The next day one of the Black men of the neighborhood, "backed up by the negroes of the community," swore an affidavit before a justice charging the two Joiner sons and two other young men. The justice and an associate were taking testimony when the report was written, and the result was not known. The inquest jury returned a verdict that Johnson had come to his death "in the hands of unknown parties." No report of an indictment or trial appears in the coverage.

The only known report is a paragraph headed "Homicide in Clay" that the Chickasaw Messenger of Okolona, Mississippi, reprinted from the Times on February 24, 1881. The paper predicted that "nothing will come of it damaging to the young men implicated," saying they had witnesses to prove they were at home. It closed with the opinion of its informant, Dr. Davis, that the killing came from "a disposition among the negroes to correct certain abuses among themselves that was hard to reach by law."

Responsibility for the killing was disputed within the single report: Black residents named the Joiner sons and two others, the paper's informant pointed to Black residents themselves, and the inquest named no one.

Four masked men killed Johnson with no lawful authority (A1); the only motive offered is the informant's opinion that Black residents were correcting 'abuses' hard to reach by law, which suggests a vigilante pretext but is not reported as fact (A1).

accounts.label: Times report via Dr. Davis
accounts.gist: Four masked men killed Johnson; the accused Joiner sons could prove they were at home, and the informant attributed the killing to Black residents correcting 'abuses' among themselves.

accounts.label: Black residents' affidavit
accounts.gist: Black neighbors charged two sons of Joe Joiner and two other young men with the killing before a justice.

accounts.label: Coroner's jury
accounts.gist: Death at the hands of unknown parties.

framing.detail: Reprinted from the Times as "Homicide in Clay"; it did not justify the killing but forecast that nothing would come of the charge and gave the informant's theory that Black residents were behind it.

versions.value: Two sons of Joe Joiner and two other young men, per the Black residents' affidavit
Black residents correcting abuses among themselves, per the informant Dr. Davis's opinion; the accused said to have alibis

conflicts.note: All three versions come from the same paragraph; the inquest verdict is the only official finding, and the paper's dismissal of the affidavit rests on its own informant.
